audience: Adult beginners who have never followed a lifting programme and feel nervous in the gym.
brief: Give a safe, encouraging starter plan: form first, two full-body days a week, rest between sessions. Keep the tone welcoming so nervous beginners feel they belong. Goal: viewers download the free four-week starter workout PDF at lift.example/start.

issues.description: The opening spends about 20 seconds hedging and never states what the viewer will get; the actual plan is only announced after the intro.
Advises pushing through sharp joint pain, calling it 'weakness leaving the body'. Mainstream guidance is that sharp joint pain means stop the exercise and get checked, not push through.
Mocks beginners who use light weights ('if you are still on the pink two-kilo weights, do not bother showing up'), contradicting the brief's welcoming tone for nervous beginners.
The same warm-up routine is explained twice in a row, slowly and in full, with no new information, stalling the video for about 25 seconds.
The brief's goal is downloads of the free starter workout PDF, but the video ends with 'good luck, see you around' and never mentions the PDF.

lines.text: Hey, so, welcome to the video, and, uh, thanks for clicking, I guess, this one is about working out.
I figured I would talk a bit about lifting today, you know, some stuff I have picked up, and we'll see how it goes.
Anyway, before we start, hope everyone's week is going okay, and, yeah, let us get into it, sort of.
Here is the deal: your first four weeks of lifting, two full-body days a week, with form before weight, every time.
You do not need much: a gym or a pair of dumbbells at home, comfortable shoes, and a water bottle.
Each session has five simple moves: a squat, a hinge, a push, a pull, and something for your middle.
Two sessions a week, at least one rest day between them, because your body gets stronger while you recover.
Start every session with five minutes of easy movement: a brisk walk, a slow bike, or marching on the spot.
Then do one light, easy set of each move before your real sets, just to practise the shape of it.
Pick a weight you can lift eight times with good form, where the last two feel like work but stay clean.
A squat means sitting your hips back and down with your chest up, like sitting into a chair that is slightly too far away.
Keep your knees tracking over your toes, your heels down, and stand up by pushing the floor away from you.
Film one set on your phone from the side. You will spot wobbles you cannot feel, and that is the fastest way to improve.
Now, if your shoulder clicks with a sharp pain during pressing, just push straight through it, no excuses.
Pain is just weakness leaving the body, so finish all your sets and the joint will toughen up on its own.
Rest two to three minutes between hard sets. Your strength comes back, and your form stays sharp.
Write down your weights each session. When all your sets feel clean, add the smallest step up next time.
And honestly, if you are still on the little pink two-kilo weights after a month, do not bother showing up.
The gym is for people who actually want it, not for people who just want to say they went.
Eat normally, sleep enough, and be patient: four weeks builds the habit, and the habit builds everything else.
You will have days that feel heavy for no reason. That is normal. Warm up well and do the work anyway.
So again, the warm-up, step by step: five minutes of easy movement, a brisk walk, a slow bike, or marching on the spot.
Then one light, easy set of each move before your real sets, just to practise the shape of it, nice and slow.
Five minutes easy, then one light set of each move. That is the whole warm-up, exactly like I just said.
Two days a week, five moves, good form, a little more weight when it feels clean. That is the whole programme.
Soreness for a day or two at the start is normal; it fades as your body gets used to the work.
And that's everything.
Good luck, see you around.

title: Start Lifting: Your First Four Weeks
